narrative:
The model estimated a 55.6% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is above the risk threshold used for this decision, so your law school application was rejected. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty: the model still estimated roughly a 44% chance of passing.

The denial was driven mainly by your third-year class standing. You are in the lowest decile, while accepted students average around the sixth decile. That very large gap was the strongest reason the prediction leaned toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor. At 36, it is slightly below the accepted-student average of about 37, but in this case it actually pushed toward passing rather than failure. Your middle family-income background was the third most influential factor and added a small push toward failure; accepted students are more often upper-middle income, although middle income is still common. Overall, the low third-year standing outweighed the favorable LSAT signal.

To improve a future application, focus on strengthening your academic record, especially evidence of improved later-year performance, and consider preparing for and retaking the LSAT to move clearly above the average. Ask admissions staff whether updated grades or scores can be submitted, whether the decision can be reconsidered or appealed, and what alternative pathways or advising support are available.
